newsitem.title: PERU: Japan calls for G7 plan to end Peru hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Japan calls for G7 plan to end Peru hostage crisis.

text.p: Japan urged the world's strongest nations on Friday to join forces to end the hostage crisis in Peru where about 20 heavily-armed Marxist guerrillas held 103 VIP captives for a 10th day.

Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda told a news conference in Tokyo that Japan has started talks with Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations to draft a common strategy to tackle the standoff at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima.

"It is clear that the international community should not condone terrorism. It is also necessary ... to act as one to help resolve this crisis by setting free all the hostages peacefully, and at an early date," Ikeda said.
Holed-up inside the fortified compound that they have booby-trapped and mined against possible attack, the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels showed no sign of giving up on Friday.

The guerrillas have freed just three hostages since the mass release of 225 captives on Sunday, keeping those they consider most useful as bargaining chips -- including two Peruvian ministers, Japanese businessmen, a handful of foreign diplomats and the brother of President Alberto Fujimori.

The president has so far rebuffed foreign offers of help and Russian leader Boris Yeltsin's earlier suggestion to send a special G7 task force to free the hostages brought no official response from Lima.
Japanese Foreign Ministry spokesman Hiroshi Hashimoto said Russia would also be included in the G7 talks adding that it was, "too early to say what specific measures could be taken."

Former hostages have warned against trying to overpower the guerrillas who are armed with grenades, explosives and ample ammunition. Defiant rebels appeared at windows several times on Thursday holding up automatic rifles and flashing victory signs to camera lenses trained on the residence.

Ikeda, who returned to Tokyo on Sunday after three days of non-stop diplomacy in Peru, reiterated Japan's support for Fujimori's handling of the crisis. The two nations had earlier clashed on how best to deal with the saga with Japanese officials initially complaining of sharp differences.

The Peruvian leader, who has spoken in public once since the rebels stormed a party at the residence on Dec 17, refuses to negotiate directly with the rebels and has rejected their main demand that the government pardon about 400 jailed comrades.
He has also ignored pleas by hostages to reconnect services to the building where the captives use flashlights after dark.

The residence remained shrouded in darkness overnight, but the evening passed without incident. A loud explosion, possibly caused by an animal stepping on a booby trap, shook the residence on Thursday night.
Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, who entered the compound for the second day on Thursday, appealed to the rebels to examine their consciences and end the siege.
"Let us hope that their hearts will be moved," said Cipriani, an outspoken critic of Peru's terrorist groups.

The latest freed hostage, Guatemalan ambassador Jose Maria Argueta, said his release on Thursday was a gesture of support by the MRTA for the peace treaty to be signed on Dec 29 between his government and the country's Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) rebels.

Recent hostage releases, particularly that of Uruguayan ambassador Tabare Bocalandro who walked free Tuesday after two jailed MRTA rebels were freed in Uruguay, have hinted that behind-the-scenes bilateral negotiations were taking place to secure the freedom of some hostages.
But Malaysia's Foreign Minister Abdullah Ahmad Badawi, who met with Fujimori on Thursday, denied suggestions he was in Lima to cut a deal for the release of his country's ambassador.
"That's not how we work. My arrival was known to the media. We can't be doing that (negotiating on our own)," Abdullah was quoted as saying in a telephone interview with the Bernama news agency.
Abdullah also added his support to Fujimori's handling of the crisis. "He (Fujimori) can control the situation. He is calm, although serious. He knows exactly what is happening."

Rumours continued to circulate in Lima about a possible asylum in Cuba for the Havana-inspired rebels. Government officials in Cuba, who have refused to condemn the attack, said they had no comment on the speculation.

All signs pointed to what Tokyo has predicted would be "a long haul" in the siege negotiations. Japanese officials said Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto would cancel a traditional New Year's break in his home constituency and may postpone foreign trips planned for January.

Isaac Velazco, the MRTA's self-styled international spokesman, told Reuters by telephone from Hamburg, Germany that his comrades in the residence would hold out for as long as it took to secure the release of rebels held in Peruvian jails.
